Question # 1:
Label the name of the Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) shown in the below
picture. Also, describe their use/function and mention the BSL levels in which
they should be used. (2+2+1=5 marks)

Solution:

Labeling and Description of Personal Protective Equipment
(PPE)
(a) Gloves
Name: Disposable Gloves
Function:

  •   Protect hands from direct contact with infectious materials, harmful chemicals, or contaminated
      surfaces.
  •   Prevent cross-contamination between patients or samples.

Use in BSL Levels:

  •   BSL-1 to BSL-4
      (Used in all biosafety levels; material and layering depend on risk level.)

(b) Safety Goggles
Name: Protective Goggles
Function:

  •   Shield eyes from chemical splashes, aerosols, or infectious droplets.
  •   Provide side protection which regular glasses lack.

Use in BSL Levels:

  •   BSL-2 to BSL-4
      (Required when there's a risk of splashes or airborne pathogens.)

(c) Surgical Mask
Name: Surgical Face Mask
Function:

  •   Protects mouth and nose from droplets.
  •   Reduces transmission of microorganisms from the wearer to the environment.

Use in BSL Levels:

  •   BSL-1 and BSL-2
      (Not suitable for protection against aerosolized agents; limited use in higher BSLs.)

(d) N95 Respirator
Name: N95 Respirator Mask
Function:

  •   Filters ≥95% of airborne particles, including pathogens.
  •   Offers a tight seal around nose and mouth, unlike surgical masks.

Use in BSL Levels:

  •   BSL-2 (aerosol-generating procedures), BSL-3
      (Not sufficient for BSL-4 unless combined with other protective gear.)

(e) Lab Coat
Name: Laboratory Coat
Function:

  •   Protects skin and clothing from chemical and biological spills.
  •   Acts as a barrier against contamination.

Use in BSL Levels:

  •   BSL-1 and BSL-2
      (BSL-3 requires solid-front or wrap-around gowns; BSL-4 uses full-body suits.)

(f) Face Shield
Name: Full Face Shield
Function:

  •   Protects entire face from splashes, sprays, and potentially infectious materials.
  •   Worn over goggles and masks for extra protection.

Use in BSL Levels:

  •   BSL-2 and BSL-3
      (Especially during procedures with high splash risk.)

(g) Respirator with Exhalation Valve
Name: Reusable Respirator (e.g., P100 or other high-filtration masks)
Function:

  •   Provides high-level filtration for airborne particles.
  •   Exhalation valve helps reduce heat and moisture buildup.

Use in BSL Levels:

  •   BSL-3
      (More commonly used in high-risk aerosol-generating environments.)

(h) Full-Body PPE Suit with PAPR
Name: Positive Pressure Suit (also known as PAPR Suit)
Function:

  •   Fully encapsulated suit that provides maximum protection.
  •   Equipped with a powered air-purifying respirator (PAPR) system to ensure clean airflow.

Use in BSL Levels:

  •   BSL-4
      (Used in maximum containment labs handling deadly, aerosol-transmitted pathogens.)

(i) Full PPE Ensemble
Name: PPE Ensemble (Gloves, Gown, Goggles, and Mask)
Function:

  •   Demonstrates a standard PPE setup showing correct layering of gloves, gown/lab coat, surgical
      mask/N95, and protective goggles.
  •   Protects multiple exposure points including mucous membranes, skin, and respiratory
      pathways.

Use in BSL Levels:

  •   BSL-3
      (Used in high-risk laboratory procedures involving aerosol-transmitted pathogens, without the
      need for a full BSL-4 suit.)

Question # 2:

  a) How do you justify that the molecular weight of NaHCO₃ is 84.007 g/mol?
     (2 marks)
  b)How do you prepare a 50mM working solution (Final volume=100 mL)
     using the above 10M stock solution NaHCO₃. (3 marks)

Solution (a):
Justification of the Molecular Weight of NaHCO₃ (Sodium
Bicarbonate)
     The molecular weight (also called molar mass) of a compound is calculated by summing the
atomic masses of all atoms present in its chemical formula. For sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃), the
formula includes:

  •   1 atom of Sodium (Na)
  •   1 atom of Hydrogen (H)
  •   1 atom of Carbon (C)
  •   3 atoms of Oxygen (O)

The standard atomic weights of these elements are:

  •   Sodium (Na) = 22.989 g/mol
  •   Hydrogen (H) = 1.008 g/mol
  •   Carbon (C) = 12.011 g/mol
  •   Oxygen (O) = 15.999 g/mol

Now, calculating the molecular weight:

Molecular weight of NaHCO₃ =
22.989 (Na) + 1.008 (H) + 12.011 (C) + (15.999 × 3 for O)
= 22.989 + 1.008 + 12.011 + 47.997
= 84.005 g/mol

Due to rounding of atomic weights in periodic tables, this is commonly reported as 84.007 g/mol.

Question # 1:

  a) Label the names of Figure A, B, C, D, E, F, and G shown in the above
     picture. Write the possible methods used for sterilization of each separately
     along with principle of that sterilization technique and why it should be
     used for that particular object (1x7= 7 Marks).
  b) Write down the name of object shown in Figure H and write its function in
     the lab. (1+2=3 marks)

Solution (a):
     The following are the names of the laboratory equipment shown in Figure A to G, along with the
possible methods used for their sterilization, the principle behind each sterilization technique, and the
reason why each method is suitable for the respective object.

Figure A: Petri Dishes
  •   Sterilization Method: Autoclaving
  •   Principle: Autoclaving uses high-pressure saturated steam at 121°C for 15–20 minutes. The high
      temperature and pressure denature microbial proteins, nucleic acids, and enzymes, leading to the
      death of all forms of life, including bacteria, fungi, and spores.
  •   Why Suitable: Petri dishes, especially those made of glass, are commonly reused in microbiology
      labs for culturing bacteria and fungi. Because microbial cultures must grow in a sterile
      environment, autoclaving is essential to ensure complete sterilization. Autoclaving is safe for glass
      and can sterilize large batches at once, making it efficient and reliable.

Figure B: Test Tubes
  •   Sterilization Method: Autoclaving
  •   Principle: Steam sterilization under pressure causes irreversible coagulation and denaturation of
      proteins, thereby killing all microorganisms including spores. Steam effectively penetrates glass
      materials and distributes heat evenly.
  •   Why Suitable: Test tubes are often used to hold media, reagents, or microbial cultures. Glass test
      tubes are heat-resistant and can tolerate autoclaving without damage. This method guarantees the
      sterility of the test tubes before they are used for culturing or chemical reactions, minimizing any
      risk of contamination.

Figure C: Inoculating Loops & Spatulas
  •   Sterilization Method: Flame Sterilization
  •   Principle: Flame sterilization involves directly exposing metal instruments to an open flame, such
      as a Bunsen burner. The intense heat incinerates any adhering microorganisms through oxidative
      destruction.
  •   Why Suitable: Inoculating loops and spatulas are frequently used for transferring microbial
      cultures or small quantities of chemicals. Since they are often reused within a single experiment or
      between samples, flaming offers a fast, effective, and accessible way to sterilize them on the spot.
      The method ensures aseptic technique without requiring complex equipment.

Figure D: Serological Pipettes
  •   Sterilization Method: Autoclaving (for reusable pipettes) or pre-sterilized single-use pipettes
  •   Principle: Autoclaving uses moist heat under pressure to coagulate microbial proteins, resulting in
      microbial death. The heat and steam penetrate the glass pipette's surface and interior effectively.
  •   Why Suitable: Pipettes are used to measure and transfer exact liquid volumes in sterile
      procedures. Glass pipettes can be safely autoclaved and reused, while plastic ones are usually
      disposed of after use and come pre-sterilized. Autoclaving reusable pipettes eliminates all
      microbial contaminants and prevents cross-contamination in sensitive procedures like tissue
      culture or media preparation.

Figure E: Micropipette Tips in Tip Boxes
  •   Sterilization Method: Autoclaving
  •   Principle: High-pressure steam at 121°C destroys microbial cells and spores through protein
      denaturation and disruption of cellular structures.
  •   Why Suitable: Micropipette tips are used in highly sensitive molecular biology techniques, such
      as PCR, DNA extraction, and enzyme assays. Even minimal contamination can lead to inaccurate
      results or complete experimental failure. Sterile tips prevent contamination of samples and
      reagents. Tip boxes containing autoclavable tips are sterilized in advance and kept sealed until use
      to maintain aseptic conditions.

Figure F: Laminar Air Flow Cabinet
  •   Sterilization Method: UV Sterilization and Surface Disinfection
  •   Principle: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation (typically UV-C at 254 nm) causes the formation of thymine
      dimers in microbial DNA, leading to mutations and ultimately cell death. UV rays are effective in
      inactivating a wide range of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, and viruses.
  •   Why Suitable: Laminar air flow cabinets are designed to provide a sterile working area by
      filtering air through HEPA filters. Before and after use, UV light is used to sterilize the work
      surface. Surface disinfectants are also used to clean the interior physically. This combination
      ensures the prevention of any microbial contamination during critical laboratory work such as cell
      culture, media preparation, and aseptic transfer of materials.

Figure G: Buffer Solution Bottle
  •   Sterilization Method: Filtration (Membrane Filtration)

  •   Principle: Membrane filtration involves passing the solution through a filter with tiny pores
      (usually 0.22 µm), which physically removes bacteria and other microorganisms without the need
      for heat. The method relies on the size exclusion principle—microbes are larger than the filter
      pores and thus get trapped.
  •   Why Suitable: Buffer solutions often contain heat-sensitive chemicals, such as Tris, EDTA, or

Key differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells:
1. Nuclear Organization
       o Prokaryotes: Lack a true nucleus; DNA lies in the nucleoid region without a
          surrounding membrane.
       o Eukaryotes: Possess a membrane-bound nucleus that encloses their genetic
          material.
2. Chromosome Structure
       o Prokaryotes: Typically have a single, circular chromosome (plus optional
          plasmids).
       o Eukaryotes: Contain multiple, linear chromosomes associated with histone
          proteins.
3. Membrane-Bound Organelles
       o Prokaryotes: Do not have membrane-bound organelles; all metabolic processes
          occur in the cytoplasm or at the cell membrane.
       o Eukaryotes: Have a variety of distinct organelles (e.g., mitochondria,
          endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, chloroplasts in plants).
4. Ribosome Size
       o Prokaryotes: Possess 70S ribosomes (composed of 50S and 30S subunits).
       o Eukaryotes: Possess larger 80S ribosomes (composed of 60S and 40S subunits)
          in the cytosol, plus 70S ribosomes in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
5. Cell Size
       o Prokaryotes: Generally small, about 0.1–5.0 µm in diameter.
       o Eukaryotes: Larger, typically 10–100 µm in diameter.
6. Cell Division
       o Prokaryotes: Divide by binary fission—a relatively simple process of DNA
          replication and cytoplasmic splitting.
       o Eukaryotes: Divide by mitosis (for growth/repair) and meiosis (for sexual
          reproduction), involving complex spindle formation and chromosome
          segregation.
7. Cell Wall Composition
       o Prokaryotes: Many (especially bacteria) have peptidoglycan-based cell walls;
          archaea have pseudopeptidoglycan or other polymers.
       o Eukaryotes: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose; fungi have chitin; animal cells
          lack a rigid cell wall.
8. Gene Structure and Processing
       o Prokaryotes: Genes are typically uninterrupted (no introns); transcription and
          translation can occur simultaneously.
       o Eukaryotes: Genes often contain introns and exons; primary transcripts undergo
          capping, polyadenylation, and splicing before translation.
9. Flagella and Motility
       o Prokaryotes: Flagella are simple helical filaments rotated by a basal motor—a
          “propeller” mechanism.
       o Eukaryotes: Flagella and cilia have a “9+2” microtubule arrangement and move
          via bending powered by dynein arms.
10. Cytoskeleton

Question# 2:
While preparing a solution you have mistakenly raised the volume of solution than the
intended volume. Can you check the new molarity of solution? If YES, explain how you
will determine it with an example and if NO, explain the reason? (5 marks)
Yes, you can determine the new molarity when volume is increased. Here's how:
Formula: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂
(Where M₁ = initial molarity, V₁ = initial volume, M₂ = new molarity, V₂ = new volume)
Example:
Initial solution: 2M NaCl, 100mL
Accidentally increased to: 150mL
Calculation:
1. Rearrange formula to solve for M₂:
 M₂ = (M₁V₁)/V₂
2. Plug in values:
 M₂ = (2M × 100mL)/150mL
3. Solve:
 M₂ = 1.33M
This works because:
- Total moles of solute remain constant
- Only volume changes
- Concentration decreases proportionally as volume increases
The solution is now more dilute (1.33M) than the intended concentration (2M).

                                        Practical No. 1
             Introduction to laboratory safety, containment and decontamination

Introduction:

       Biotechnology is the use of an organism, or a component of an organism or other
biological system, to make a product or process for a specific use. Biotechnological techniques
are applicable not only to modern medical practice but also to the production of genetically
modified    organisms,    forensics,   and    quality   assessment     of   laboratory   animals,
pharmacogenomics, and other fields. Many applications of modern biotechnology depend on
the ability to analyze, manipulate, and cut and paste pieces of DNA. Approaches that involve
sequencing and manipulation of DNA are sometimes referred to as DNA technology.

Safety Considerations:

    Use personal protective equipment such as disposable gloves, lab coats, disposable
       masks, etc.
    Handle all sharps with care and dispose of sharps in the sharp’s disposal containers.
    Handle hazardous chemicals and samples carefully. Blood and other body fluid must be
       considered potentially hazardous. Biological waste should be disposed of in the designated
       trash bags that could be incinerated later on.
    Decontaminate the work benches regularly and especially before and after work. For
       decontamination, wipe the surfaces with 10% bleach followed by water.

Containments: Containment is defined as the action of confining within a defined space a
microbiological agent or other entity that is being cultured, stored, manipulated, transported, or
destroyed in order to prevent or limit its contact with people and/or the environment.

Decontamination: Decontamination is a combination of processes that removes or destroys
contamination so that infectious agents or other contaminants cannot reach a susceptible site in
sufficient quantities to initiate infection, or other harmful response. Its types include, Physical
cleaning, Ultrasonication, Disinfection, Antisepsis, Sterilizations.

                                        Practical No. 1
             Introduction to laboratory safety, containment and decontamination

Introduction:

       Biotechnology is the use of an organism, or a component of an organism or other
biological system, to make a product or process for a specific use. Biotechnological techniques
are applicable not only to modern medical practice but also to the production of genetically
modified    organisms,    forensics,   and    quality   assessment     of   laboratory   animals,
pharmacogenomics, and other fields. Many applications of modern biotechnology depend on
the ability to analyze, manipulate, and cut and paste pieces of DNA. Approaches that involve
sequencing and manipulation of DNA are sometimes referred to as DNA technology.

Safety Considerations:

    Use personal protective equipment such as disposable gloves, lab coats, disposable
       masks, etc.
    Handle all sharps with care and dispose of sharps in the sharp’s disposal containers.
    Handle hazardous chemicals and samples carefully. Blood and other body fluid must be
       considered potentially hazardous. Biological waste should be disposed of in the designated
       trash bags that could be incinerated later on.
    Decontaminate the work benches regularly and especially before and after work. For
       decontamination, wipe the surfaces with 10% bleach followed by water.

Containments: Containment is defined as the action of confining within a defined space a
microbiological agent or other entity that is being cultured, stored, manipulated, transported, or
destroyed in order to prevent or limit its contact with people and/or the environment.

Decontamination: Decontamination is a combination of processes that removes or destroys
contamination so that infectious agents or other contaminants cannot reach a susceptible site in
sufficient quantities to initiate infection, or other harmful response. Its types include, Physical
cleaning, Ultrasonication, Disinfection, Antisepsis, Sterilizations.

Glassware
       The glassware needs to be selected according to its accuracy and capacity. Narrow neck
glassware is more accurate by rule. Some glassware can be used to measure fixed volumes while
others can be used to measure a variety of volumes. Some glassware used in laboratory are enlisted;
      Bulb and graduated pipettes. These are used to transport specific amounts of fluids from
       one place to another.

                                       Bulb and graduated pipettes

      Burettes. These are used to dispense exact quantities of liquid into another vessel.

                                             4

                                                 Burettes

   Beakers. Simple containers used to hold samples and reagents.

                                              Beaker

   Volumetric flasks. Similar to beakers, these are used to hold samples but usually come in
    a conical or spherical shape with a tapering neck.

                                        Volumetric flasks

   Funnels. The tapered neck of a funnel allows easy pouring of a liquid into a narrow orifice.

                                             5

                                              Funnel

   Graduated Cylinders. Similar to beakers, these cylindrical vessels have volumetric
    markings to allow for monitoring volume.

                                       Graduated cylinders

   Vials. Small bottles used to store samples or reagents.

      Stirring Rods. Used to mix solvents and samples together.
